articles.title: India rest Ishan Kishan for 3rd T20I vs NZ as precautionary measure
articles.summary:
Injured wicketkeeper-batter Ishan Kishan will be unavailable for the third T20 International against New Zealand as a precautionary measure, India's bowling coach Morne Morkel said on Monday.
The 28-year-old had suffered a right adductor strain during the series-opener last week.
"Ishan is doing well. He will be training today. For tomorrow, I think he is not available for selection, just as a precaution," Morkel said at the pre-match press conference here.
Right adductor is a group of muscles located on the inner side of the thigh.
Kishan had missed the second T20I as well, with teenage batting sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi replacing him in the playing XI.
Uncapped wicketkeeper-batter Kumar Kushagra was added to the squad as cover for Kishan. India lead the five-match series 2-0.

articles.summary: Michigan: US President Donald Trump, offering an early glimpse into the Republican Party's political future, named JD Vance and Marco Rubio among the prominent figures who could run for the White House in 2028, boasting that the GOP possesses a "great bench" compared to the Democrats.In an interview with FOX 2's Roop Raj ahead of Michigan rally, when asked directly about who might launch a presidential bid in 2028, Trump stated that while it is premature to name an outright front-runner, the party has no shortage of strong candidates."I could tell you who I think, but it's a little bit early," Trump said."We have great names - you have JD Vance, Marco Rubio, and many others. The outcome will have significant implications for Trump's legislative agenda and the balance of political power in Washington.United States midterm elections are nationwide votes held every four years at the exact midpoint of a president's term. Acting as a major political temperature check for the country, these elections determine control of the federal government by putting all 435 seats in the House of Representatives and about one-third of the Senate up for grabs.The political contest comes amid broader challenges for the administration, including economic concerns and declining approval ratings. The Wall Street Journal reported in September that Trump's approval rating had fallen to 37 per cent in its polling, a low for a president heading into midterm elections in the publication's polling history dating back to 1990.

articles.title: What's got Europe angry? Protests sweep nations
articles.summary: Protests over the cost of living, strained public services and political accountability swept across France, Italy, Belgium and Albania on Saturday, with demonstrators clashing with police in several cities and authorities deploying tear gas, water cannons and large numbers of officers to contain unrest.The demonstrations reflected different domestic grievances but a common pattern of mounting public frustration, particularly over education, economic hardship and trust in political leadership. France saw the largest mobilisation, with more than 400,000 people taking to the streets nationwide, according to the Interior Ministry, while Albania witnessed a fresh escalation of anti-government protests after days of violence in its capital, Tirana.Also read: More than 400,000 protest across France, challenging Macron as Paris clashes eruptItaly saw renewed demonstrations against war and rising living costs, with clashes in Turin, Rome and Bologna, while hundreds of mainly young protesters gathered in Brussels to demand better conditions in education and challenge police conduct.The latest unrest follows a week of violence in France and Belgium, as authorities across the four countries grapple with demonstrations that have increasingly tested public order and political leadership.France: School funding and living costs fuel mass mobilisationMore than 400,000 people rallied across France on Saturday against school funding shortages and soaring living costs, posing a fresh challenge to President Emmanuel Macron's government in the final months of his presidency.The Interior Ministry estimated nationwide participation at 410,000, including 110,000 in Paris, while the CGT trade union put the figure at nearly 800,000. The Paris march began peacefully but ended in clashes near Porte de Vincennes, where some protesters threw projectiles and police deployed tear gas and water cannons.The Paris prosecutor's office said 64 people had been arrested in connection with the demonstration, including six minors, and 40 had been placed in police custody. The government had deployed up to 70,000 officers nationwide, supported by helicopters, armoured vehicles and water cannons.What began last month as a protest over staff shortages at a high school southeast of Paris has grown into a broader movement involving students and workers seeking better education, higher wages and improved pensions.Public middle and high schools lost 15.4 million teaching hours in the 2024-25 school year because absent teachers were not replaced, amounting to 7.5% of scheduled teaching time, according to Education Ministry figures.Students are demanding 250,000 additional higher-education places, more teachers, school repairs and increased student grants. They are also seeking a freeze on rents in public student housing.Economic pressures have added to the anger. French energy prices rose 21.3% in September from a year earlier, helping push overall inflation to 3.1%, according to national statistics agency INSEE.The unrest has become a test of Macron's authority, with the far-right National Rally accusing his government of failing to protect the public. Authorities banned demonstrations in several cities, including Lyon, Nice and Montpellier, drawing criticism from trade unions over freedom of expression.Also read: Italy sees fresh protests over war, cost of living as Police brace for violenceItaly: Anti-war rallies return as police brace for violenceItalian cities saw fresh protests against war and rising living costs on Saturday, a week after demonstrations escalated into clashes, looting and property damage.Turin, Rome and Bologna witnessed confrontations between police and demonstrators, while protests in Milan were largely peaceful, Reuters reported. Police maintained a heavy presence and many shops shut as a precaution against potential damage.Authorities strengthened security after calls for further demonstrations circulated on social media, seeking to prevent a repeat of the previous weekend's violence. Reuters witnesses did not observe shops being looted or property vandalised during Saturday's demonstrations.Earlier in the day, Italian police said they had detained a person allegedly linked to organising the 'October 17 Movement', associated with last weekend's protests, and taken the individual to police headquarters in Milan for questioning.The demonstrations brought together grievances over international conflict and the rising cost of living, although the reports did not establish a single nationwide political demand driving the rallies.Belgium: Young protesters clash with police over educationIn Brussels, hundreds of mainly young demonstrators gathered on Saturday to demand better conditions in education, continuing a series of rallies held over recent months.Police used tear gas and pepper spray as clashes broke out, with protesters accusing authorities of excessive violence and calling for greater education funding, Reuters witnesses and Belgian media reported.In one incident witnessed by Reuters, police pursued demonstrators who ran and fell to the ground, while officers hit and kicked one protester. Elsewhere, demonstrators threw road signs and other objects onto a pile of rental scooters and bicycles and attempted to set it alight.Belgian media also reported that police used tear gas to disperse a group of protesters.The clashes were smaller and less violent than those seen in Belgium the previous week and in neighbouring France, Reuters reported.Brussels police said no major incidents had occurred by the end of the afternoon. Officers temporarily detained five people for disturbing public order and four others over alleged possession of prohibited weapons and incitement to rioting.Albania: Anti-government anger widens beyond original grievancesThousands gathered in Tirana on Saturday for a fresh anti-government demonstration, as unrest that has shaken the Albanian capital since mid-October escalated again after several quieter days.Police fired tear gas, used water cannons and rubber bullets after some demonstrators threw stones at the education ministry, a focal point of the protests. Several government buildings have been attacked during the unrest, and authorities say more than 300 protesters and police officers have been injured. Dozens of demonstrators have also been detained.The movement has expanded beyond its original grievances into a broader campaign against corruption, poor public services and Prime Minister Edi Rama's government.Anti-government protests began in May over a luxury hotel project linked to US President Donald Trump's family. Scientists said in July that the development had already caused irreparable damage to a previously pristine stretch of Albania's coastline. Anger over the project subsequently broadened into demands for Rama to step down.Students have raised concerns about deteriorating education standards and limited opportunities, while economic hardship and emigration have added to public frustration. More than 1.5 million people have left Albania since the fall of Communism in the 1990s, leaving a population of about 2.3 million.

Both had supported the movement from the start, but this was their first protest together."The young people who have been demonstrating have not been heard, and as a parent and as a teacher, I stand with them," Pittion said.Garance said she had been "really scared" to attend after seeing images of last weekend's violence, but argued that staying away would hand the government a victory.Public middle and high schools lost 15.4 million teaching hours in the 2024-25 school year because absent teachers were not replaced, according to Education Ministry figures. Authorities had banned rallies in cities including Lyon, Nice and Montpellier.Trade unions have criticized the bans, calling them violations of freedom of expression, which is protected by the constitution.Thousands also marched Saturday in Orleans, south of Paris, in a separate peaceful protest against the far right as Marine Le Pen's National Rally held a two-day congress in the city.Macron, a centrist, has entered the crisis in the final stretches of his term with his popularity at its lowest since he took office in 2017. He has said that the measures are needed to protect city centers, businesses and public buildings.Nunez acknowledged Monday that police had lost control in some cities during last weekend's unrest, when more than half a million people took to the streets and some 3,000 shops across France were damaged or looted amid street violence not seen in years.He offered to resign, but Macron refused the offer.Shops board up and museums closeGendarmes stood guard Saturday beneath the Arc de Triomphe and shopkeepers boarded up storefronts across Paris. Near the Saint-Lazare train station Saturday, Akram Ahmed, a 34-year-old contractor, was boarding up an optician's shop."I got the call last night," he said. "The owner seemed desperate. He said I was saving his life."Major museums, including the Louvre, Orsay Museum, Picasso Museum and Grand Palais - where a major Cezanne exhibit is on display - were shuttered Saturday.Art Basel, one of the world's most prestigious contemporary art fairs, opened to the public Friday, but only for the day, with the threat of unrest prompting organizers to cancel the weekend program.Students and workers are angryStudent groups want 250,000 more places in higher education and an end to selection through Parcoursup, the national admissions system.Their joint 10-point plan also calls for more teachers and repairs to schools and universities.They are also seeking help with everyday costs: an extra 200 euros ($224) a month in student grants and a rent freeze in public student housing.Energy prices in France were 21.3% higher in September than a year earlier, helping drive overall inflation to 3.1%, according to the national statistics agency, INSEE.Paris protester Louis Ledoux--Xatard voiced frustration over inequality."Looking at countries like the United States, we don't want to end up like them, where part of the population has everything and the others have nothing," he said."I never imagined that I'd be taking to the streets so much before my thirties."

articles.title: Italy sends more soldiers to Milan as European cities brace for protests
articles.summary:
Italy deployed soldiers to Milan as the nation's fashion and finance capital expected fresh protests on Saturday, one week after looting and clashes with police.
Premier Giorgia Meloni announced a raft of measures, including sending an additional 500 soldiers to Milan and tougher penalties for minors, who police said made up a large part of the violent protesters.
While protests in France have claimed most international attention, Milan is among the many other European cities where protests are also scheduled Saturday, from Portugal to Albania.
Milan
---------
The 500 soldiers deployed to Milan come in addition to hundreds already stationed there, and will support about 5,000 police and other law enforcement personnel. Authorities are conducting drone surveillance, checks at railway stations, rapid-response units and online monitoring for potential calls to violence.
